blocks.text: It is proved that שרף saraph is the hydrus and chersydrus; those bitten by which, the Israelites, were healed by the sight of the bronze serpent.

The שרף saraph also deserves our discussion, since it was a type of Christ, Num. XXI, 9. Ioh. III, 14., and since it shares its name with the noblest of the angels, Es. VI, 2. Moreover, it alone among serpents is said to fly, Es. XIV, 29. (var. XV, 2.) and XXX, 6. There מעופף refers to true flight, not to leaping, as the Hebrews wrongly write. The Sacred Writers mention two places in which it chiefly breeds, namely Arabia Deserta, Deut. VIII, 15., and Egypt, Es. XXX, 6. The name is derived from burning: either because of its fiery colour, which the bronze serpent would have reproduced (so Vatablus), or because it burns with its breath and bite. R. Selomo, on Numbers XXI: את הנחשים השרפים ששורפים את האדם בארס שיניהם, The serpents were called seraphim because they burned a man with the poison of their teeth. And on Es. XXX, of the serpent saraph: וזרק להב מפיו, It scatters flame from its mouth. And Kimchi in his Lexicon: נקראים כן לפי שהם שורפים בהבל פיהם, They are so called because they burn with the breath of their mouth. For a not dissimilar reason those angels were called שרפים seraphim (that is, as Dionysius ^{a)} and Cyril ^{b)} interpret it, ἐμπρησταὶ, ἤτοι θερμαίνοντες [emprēstai, ētoi thermainontes]), one of whom cleansed the lips of the prophet Isaiah with a coal taken from the altar. The Greeks, too, name certain serpents πρηστῆρας [prēstēras] and καύσωνας [kausōnas], likewise from burning. This was the reason why certain recent interpreters [col. 422] rendered the Hebrew שרף saraph as prester and causon, words which correspond exactly to the Hebrew if one considers their origin. For anyone who compares the versions of the Greeks with the source will at once notice that the verb שרף is the same as ἐμπρῆσαι [emprēsai] or κατακαῦσαι [katakausai]. But one must not cling so stubbornly to etymologies [III, 212] that the thing itself is meanwhile neglected. Since it is common to very different serpents that they burn with breath or bite, why could a name taken from this not apply to various species of serpents? What of the fact that the Greeks themselves do not know what kind of serpent the prester is? For some confuse the prester with the dipsas, as Dioscorides and Aegineta do; others make it distinct, as Lucan and Solinus do. And what Aelian thought here nobody could easily say, since in one place he seems to side with Dioscorides, in another with Lucan. Therefore those who interpret שרף saraph by so doubtful and ambiguous a word rather obscure the matter than explain it.

To me, weighing everything, it seems most probable that שרף saraph is the hydrus or chersydrus. These two differ little from each other. For what had been a hydrus in winter, while there was water in the pools, is forced to live on dry land after the water has failed in the heat, and so becomes a chersydrus, that is, a hydrus living ἐν χέρσῳ [en chersō], on dry land. Then indeed, tormented by thirst in hot regions, it has a far sharper and more harmful poison. Hence the Poet ^{c)}:
After the marsh is drained and the earth gapes with heat, it leaps out onto the dry ground and, rolling its flaming eyes, rages in the fields, fierce with thirst and maddened by the heat.

Aëtius, Tetrab. 4, Serm. 1, ch. 35: The chersydrus, living on land, becomes fiercer than itself. In moist places, sated with moist food, it does not have pure poison; but when it is terrestrial, it acquires it in its most undiluted and more harmful form. Therefore it then burns up with its bite whatever it touches. Nicander on those bitten by the chersydrus, Theriaca, line 363:
— — — τὰ δ' ἄλγεα φωτὰ δαμάζει Μυρία πυρπολέοντα· θοῶς δ' ἐπὶ γυῖα χέονται Πρηδόνες. — — — — — [ta d' algea phōta damazei / Myria pyrpoleonta; thoōs d' epi guia cheontai / Prēdones.]

Countless pains overpower the men, ravaging them as with fires; and at once burning pustules spread over the limbs. For that is properly πρηδόνες [prēdones]. Aëtius: In those bitten there occurs swelling, continuous burning pain, etc. Avicenna ^{d)}: تاخذ اللسعة بوجع شديد وتلتهب [taʾkhudh al-lasʿa bi-wajaʿ shadīd wa-taltahib] The bite begins with violent pain, and becomes inflamed. Others in Gesner report that on a rod brought to its mouth blisters are raised, or pustules of the colour of bile; and that a sword, from the point to the hilt, is stained a foul blue colour, as if seized by a violent flame; likewise that this poison has a fiery force, and therefore always seeks the upper parts. The poets imagine that Hercules was consumed by this fire when he had put on a garment dipped in the poison of the Lernaean Hydra. Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 9, Fable 3: [III, 213] The very blood hisses, as a glowing plate once dipped in a cold pool, and boils with the burning poison. There is no limit: the greedy flames suck up his vitals, dark-blue sweat flows from his whole body, his scorched sinews crackle, the devouring fire roams in the depths of his lungs and feeds through all his limbs.
